opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's really the heart of the business model when you lease robots. When a customer leases from us rather than buying outright, they're not just paying for a piece of hardware. They're paying for an outcome: the robot shows up, it works, and it keeps working. So the service obligation is ours, not theirs, and we have to build the whole company around that.

In practice, a few things matter. First is uptime. We think about it the way a utility would. If a robot goes down on a customer's floor, that's lost productivity for them, so we need to know before they do. That means remote monitoring and telemetry on every unit. We're watching battery health, motor currents, error logs, and how often the robot is asking for help. A lot of the time we can spot a problem developing and swap a part or push a software fix before it ever turns into downtime.

Second is the field service model. You can't fly an engineer out every time something hiccups, or the economics fall apart. So we design for serviceability from the start. We use modular components that a technician, or sometimes even the customer's own staff with a bit of guidance, can swap in minutes. We also keep spare units and parts staged regionally, so if something serious happens we can just replace the robot and fix the broken one back at our facility.

Third, and people underestimate this one, is software. A leased robot gets better over time because we keep shipping updates: better navigation, new capabilities, improved safety behavior. That's part of what the customer is paying for, and it's also how we drive down our own service costs, because every fix we make applies across the whole fleet.

The flip side is that leasing forces discipline on us. If the robot is unreliable, we eat the cost, not the customer. That aligns our incentives with theirs. We're motivated to build machines that last and to learn from every failure in the field. Honestly, I think that alignment is one of the big reasons robots-as-a-service has taken off. It takes the risk off the customer and puts it on the people best positioned to manage it, which is us.

r001.rationale: The response discusses monitoring, repairs, replacement robots, and the company bearing reliability costs, but does not state a contractual commitment to have a human perform the robot’s task while it is down.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that when you lease a robot, you're not really selling a machine at all—you're selling uptime. The customer doesn't care that they have a robot on the floor. They care that the work gets done, every shift, without them having to become robotics experts. So the service obligation isn't a line item bolted onto the deal; it's the actual product.

That changes how you build and how you operate. On the engineering side, it means designing for maintainability from day one—modular components that a field tech can swap in minutes, remote diagnostics so we see a problem before the customer does, and software that can be updated over the air without someone flying out. If I'm eating the cost of every failure, I'm suddenly very motivated to make failures rare and cheap to fix.

On the operational side, it means committing to real response times and actually staffing to meet them. We think a lot about where our customers are, where our spare parts are, and how fast we can get a person on site when remote support isn't enough. We also try to be honest in the contract about what "up" means—how we measure it, what counts as our fault versus theirs, and what happens if we miss. Customers can live with a lot if the expectations are clear.

The last piece is that the data flows back into the roadmap. Every service call is a lesson. If the same part keeps failing at a certain site, that's an engineering problem, not just a support problem. So we close that loop tightly. Over time, the fleet gets more reliable, our service costs come down, and the customer sees it as a partner relationship rather than a vendor they have to chase.

r001.rationale: The response discusses response times, onsite technical support, and contract terms for measuring uptime, but it does not say the company contractually commits to a human performing the robot’s task while the robot is down.

astra-6.text: I think you have to look at it as an ongoing commitment to the customer. They’re leasing a robot because they need a job done, so getting it installed is just the beginning. You’ve got to support it, keep it running, and respond when something goes wrong. That means thinking about service from the start—how you diagnose problems, how you repair the robot, and how you minimize downtime. The customer is counting on that capability every day, and the service has to reflect that.

r001.rationale: The response describes supporting, repairing, and minimizing downtime, but does not state that the company contractually provides a human to perform the robot’s task while it is down.

sol-6.1.text: When you lease a robot to a customer, you’re taking responsibility for keeping it working. You can’t just drop it off and say, “Call us if there’s a problem.” You have to think about maintenance, support, and what happens when something breaks. How quickly can you get them running again? Because the customer is counting on that robot to do a job. So I approach service as part of the product itself. The lease has to support that ongoing commitment, and we have to be prepared to deliver on it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses maintenance, support, and getting the robot running after a breakdown, but does not state that the company contractually commits to having a human perform the robot’s task while it is down.
